nameStory: This fungus doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists simply call it by its Latin name, Arthrophaga myriapodina. The name tells its story perfectly: 'Arthrophaga' means 'joint-eater' (referring to the segmented bodies of its victims), while 'myriapodina' points to its target hosts - the myriapods, which include millipedes and centipedes.
description: Arthrophaga myriapodina is a parasitic fungus that lives inside millipedes, slowly consuming them from within. You won't see this fungus growing on trees or soil like mushrooms - instead, you'll encounter it as white, fuzzy growths emerging from dead or dying millipedes. The fungus is microscopic when it first infects its host, but becomes visible as cotton-like patches when the millipede dies. It's part of a specialized group of fungi that have evolved specifically to parasitize insects and other small arthropods.

idTips.label: Host millipede behavior
idTips.description: Look for millipedes that have climbed unusually high on plants, rocks, or fence posts before dying - this bizarre 'zombie' behavior is the fungus hijacking the millipede's brain to spread its spores from an elevated position

idTips.label: White fungal growth
idTips.description: Dead millipedes will show fluffy white or cream-colored fungal threads emerging from between their body segments, feeling cotton-soft if you gently touch them with a stick

idTips.label: Host species
idTips.description: Most commonly found on the yellow-spotted millipede (Apheloria virginiensis) and related species - look for the distinctive bright yellow warning spots on dark millipede bodies

idTips.label: Location of death
idTips.description: Infected millipedes are often found dead while clinging to vertical surfaces like tree bark, plant stems, or rocks, rather than curled up on the ground like naturally deceased millipedes

habitat: Found throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests, particularly in areas with rich leaf litter where millipedes thrive. Look in moist woodland areas under logs, rocks, and fallen leaves where millipedes naturally live and feed on decaying organic matter. The fungus is most likely encountered along hiking trails and in suburban areas where millipedes are common.

seasonality.spring: Active as millipedes emerge from winter dormancy. Look for infected millipedes beginning to show unusual climbing behavior as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when fungal infections are most visible. Dead millipedes with white fungal growth are most commonly spotted during warm, humid weather.
seasonality.fall: Continued activity as millipedes remain active. Late-season infections may be visible on millipedes preparing for winter.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive in New England's cold climate. Both the fungus and its millipede hosts enter dormancy during freezing weather.

funFact: This fungus essentially turns millipedes into zombies - it hijacks their nervous system and forces them to climb as high as possible before death, turning the millipede's own body into a spore-launching tower to infect more victims below!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other types of mold or fungus growing on dead millipedes, but the key difference is the 'zombie climbing' behavior - if you find a millipede that died in an unnaturally high position with white fuzzy growth, it's likely this specific parasitic fungus rather than random decay.
contextualKnowledge: This belongs to a fascinating group of fungi called entomopathogens (insect-killing fungi) that have inspired zombie movies and video games. Unlike the friendly fungi we see as mushrooms, these are specialized biological weapons that have co-evolved with their arthropod hosts over millions of years.
compareHints: As the only known species in its genus, Arthrophaga myriapodina is unique among New England's parasitic fungi for specifically targeting millipedes. Other entomopathogenic fungi in the region typically infect insects like ants, flies, or caterpillars, but this species has specialized exclusively on millipedes and closely related myriapods. Its 'zombie climbing' behavior is shared with some ant-infecting fungi but is rare among millipede parasites.
